solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: After cheap exercises, boy's facing head

indicators.note: to exercise something is to work it over and put it through its paces, so these letters get reworked
the word after places the first piece at the end, following the reworked letters

explanation.surface: A lad heads off after doing some cheap workouts.
explanation.walkthrough: CEPHALAD is an anatomical term, the opposite of caudad; the boy's possessive is just glue.
explanation.definitionFit: Cephalad is the anatomical adverb meaning towards or pointing in the direction of the skull end of the body.

clue.text: Di's ignored in debate, a stubborn one

indicators.note: something ignored is left out of account, so those letters are dropped from the longer word

blocks.note: the name with its possessive, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Di is left out of the discussion by an obstinate participant.
explanation.walkthrough: Take DIS from the front of DISCUSS to leave CUSS.
explanation.definitionFit: A cuss is an informal word for a person, usually a perverse or awkward character who will not budge.

clue.text: Recalling paean, I can pine if endlessly out of sorts

indicators.note: without its end, the short word loses its final letter and keeps only its start
out of sorts means disordered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone moping and unwell recalls a hymn of praise.
explanation.definitionFit: Epinician describes a Greek ode celebrating a victory, a song of triumph much like a paean.

clue.text: Circumlocutory, awful chipper about opening of red wine

indicators.note: something awful is in a bad state, so these letters are put in a new order
the opening of a word is its first letter
about means around, so the reworked letters surround the rest

blocks.note: Asti is an Italian sparkling wine

explanation.surface: A cheerful drinker in a terrible state rambles round the point once the red is opened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chipper' looks like a mood, but it is the fodder; its rearranged letters wrap around the other two pieces with one letter left over at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Periphrastic speech uses many words where few would do, which is exactly a roundabout, circumlocutory way of expressing something.

clue.text: Army mostly found accepting religious instruction repellent

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter
accepting means taking in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a horde is a great army or crowd

explanation.surface: Soldiers are discovered taking a scripture lesson, which they find distasteful.
explanation.walkthrough: HORDE mostly is HORD, which takes in RI to make HORRID. RI is the British school abbreviation for religious instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Horrid and repellent are synonyms, both describing something so unpleasant that it provokes disgust or aversion.

clue.text: Call for humour when it's missing

indicators.note: when something is missing it is absent, so those letters are taken away

explanation.surface: Demanding a joke when the moment lacks one.
explanation.walkthrough: LEVITY without IT leaves LEVY.
explanation.definitionFit: To levy is to demand or impose a payment, such as a tax or troops, so it means to call for them.

clue.text: Time for start of struggle grated awfully (6, two words)

indicators.note: done awfully means done badly, so the letters come out in a jumbled order

explanation.surface: The moment a fight began, nerves were badly jangled.
explanation.walkthrough: Der Tag is German for 'the day', used of the long-awaited day of a decisive conflict.
explanation.definitionFit: Der Tag was the German toast to the day war against Britain would begin, so it names the moment hostilities start.

clue.text: E.g. Homeric events, read in repose

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the following word

explanation.surface: Reading the adventures of Homer's heroes while relaxing.
explanation.definitionFit: An epos is an epic poem, the form of the Iliad and Odyssey, whose deeds are read as a narrative.

clue.text: Permission for e.g. bishop outside to dine

blocks.note: ex means out of or outside

explanation.surface: A cleric is allowed to go out for dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: An exeat is the leave a bishop grants a priest to work outside his diocese, as well as a school's leave of absence.
explanation.definitionFit: Exeat is Latin for 'let him go out', the formal leave of absence granted, among others, to clergy by a bishop.

clue.text: Describing certain fossils, depiction ran awry

indicators.note: awry means askew or gone wrong, so the letters are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A drawing of fossils turned out badly.
explanation.definitionFit: Pentacrinoid describes the stalked larval stage of feather stars, resembling the fossil crinoid genus Pentacrinus.

clue.text: Glasses etc, warmest when spread on middle of chest

indicators.note: spread out means scattered, so these letters are redistributed
the middle of a five-letter word is its third letter

explanation.surface: Seems to describe spectacles or a warming rub spread on the chest.
explanation.definitionFit: Stemware is the collective name for glassware with stems, such as wine glasses and goblets.

clue.text: English king in public to exercise too much?

indicators.note: in places the preceding pieces inside the following word

blocks.note: overt means open, done in public

explanation.surface: An English monarch working out in public, perhaps too hard.
explanation.walkthrough: The English king goes inside the public word after its first two letters, not at its edge.
explanation.definitionFit: To overexert oneself is to strain or work beyond safe limits, which is pushing exercise too far.

clue.text: Bishop always replacing line in quiet? It was waste

indicators.note: replacing says the new pieces take the place of one letter in the word

explanation.surface: A bishop forever demanding silence in church.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir-reverence was an old apology before mentioning something filthy, and so came to mean excrement; hence the past tense. RR, Right Reverend, is a bishop's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir-reverence is an obsolete euphemism for human excrement, so in old usage the word denoted bodily waste.

clue.text: Exercises rolling over yielding a chortle from Mac

indicators.note: yielding means giving up, so the following letter is surrendered
something rolling over is turned end to end, so it is read backwards

blocks.note: exercises, as a verb, means trains

explanation.surface: A Scot chuckles while doing rolling exercises.
explanation.walkthrough: TRAINS without A is TRINS; turn it round. Mac stands for a Scot, and snirt is Scots dialect.
explanation.definitionFit: A snirt is a Scots word for a suppressed laugh or snigger, which matches a chortle.

clue.text: Easy? Not half, to touch up inside forthwith

indicators.note: not half means only half the word survives, the second half going
inside places one piece within the other

blocks.note: Chambers gives tat as a verb meaning to touch or tap lightly

explanation.surface: A quick retouching job is called easy, and is wanted at once.
explanation.walkthrough: Statim is the medical prescription term, often shortened to stat.
explanation.definitionFit: Statim is Latin for immediately, used on prescriptions to mean the drug must be given at once.

clue.text: Included in rest, later treated among protuberances (9, two words)

indicators.note: something treated is processed and changed, so these letters are reworked
among puts the reworked letters inside another word

blocks.note: inia is the plural of inion, the bump at the back of the skull

explanation.surface: A patient at rest is later treated for some lumps.
explanation.walkthrough: The inion is the bony bump at the back of the skull, a word few solvers know outside Chambers.
explanation.definitionFit: Inter alia is Latin for among other things, describing an item mentioned as one included among the rest.

clue.text: Incandescent cake decoration

blocks.note: second meaning: icing squeezed through a nozzle in lines

explanation.surface: A glowing cake ornament, perhaps candles.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means extremely hot in the phrase piping hot, and also the iced lines decorators squeeze onto cakes.

clue.text: A girl mostly miscast in drama, pinching others' ideas

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter goes
a miscast actor is in the wrong role, so the letters are placed wrongly
in places the reworked letters inside the following word

explanation.surface: A young actress wrongly cast in a play steals others' lines.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the last letter of 'girl', shuffle what's left with A, and put the result into the play before its final Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Plagiary, an old word for plagiarism, is the practice of stealing and passing off another writer's work as one's own.

clue.text: Making runs in sport locally (cricket)

indicators.note: in places the single letter inside the following word

blocks.note: gig is an old word for fun or sport

explanation.surface: Scoring runs in a local game of cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed cricket looks like the game being played; it is the insect, which grig names in dialect.
explanation.definitionFit: Grig is an English dialect name for the cricket insect or grasshopper, hence the regional qualifier.

clue.text: Spenser's learned by heart – forgive one let off

indicators.note: let off means released, so those letters are freed from the word

explanation.surface: Someone who learned Spenser's verse by heart is excused.
explanation.walkthrough: Spenser's spelling COND is the past tense of con, to study or memorise.
explanation.definitionFit: Cond is Spenser's form of conned, meaning studied or memorised, in other words learned by rote.

clue.text: Univ officer broadcast on TV?

blocks.note: first meaning: Oxford and Cambridge slang for a proctor
second meaning: short for a programme

explanation.surface: A university official appearing on television.
explanation.definitionFit: Prog is university slang for a proctor, the disciplinary official, and also a casual short form of programme.

clue.text: Player, by the sound of it secretary's responsibility

indicators.note: the phrase says to go by how the word is said rather than how it is written

explanation.surface: An actor seems to take on the job of a secretary.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech the two words sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Acta are the minutes or recorded proceedings of a meeting, which keeping is a secretary's duty.

clue.text: What's wielded at Troon, to display by name

blocks.note: to air something is to show it off

explanation.surface: A golfer at Troon shows off a club bearing their name.
explanation.walkthrough: Troon is a famous Scottish golf course, and AIRN is Scots for iron, the golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: Airn is the Scots form of iron, and an iron is a club swung on golf courses such as Troon.

clue.text: Where plates are stacked in wine container set before king

indicators.note: set before puts the first piece ahead of the next one

blocks.note: a wine bin is a rack for bottles

explanation.surface: Plates are stacked in the wine rack beside the king.
explanation.walkthrough: Bink is a Scots and northern word for a bench or plate rack.
explanation.definitionFit: A bink is a dialect word for a kitchen bench or shelf, the rack on which dishes are kept.

clue.text: This one's put in to drive 'quicky' aiming high

indicators.note: something put in is placed inside, so the first piece goes into the next

blocks.note: this one, the speaker, is me
to bear can mean to drive or push, as in bear down

explanation.surface: A fast car, bought to drive at speed with ambition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quicky' is cricket slang for a fast bowler; the answer is also slang for a BMW, which the surface hints at.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a beamer is a full toss aimed at head height, a dangerous delivery from a fast bowler.

clue.text: Might she have beguiled Pascal?

indicators.note: beguiled suggests charmed and led astray, so the letters are led into a new order

explanation.surface: Wondering whether some woman charmed the philosopher Blaise Pascal.
explanation.walkthrough: Pascal must be turned into his first name before shuffling; the whole clue then describes the answer as a woman who might have charmed him.
explanation.definitionFit: Isabel is a woman's name, and the clue as a whole pictures her as someone who might have charmed the philosopher.

clue.text: Scottish border – it divides one such heading north

indicators.note: in a down entry, heading north means reading upwards, so backwards
something that divides another sits in the middle of it

blocks.note: a border, one like the defined thing

explanation.surface: A Scottish boundary splits a region heading north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One such' refers back to the definition: a border, here a hem.
explanation.definitionFit: Meith is a Scots word for a boundary or landmark, so it denotes a border.

clue.text: Long for reeds scattered round island

indicators.note: scattered things are strewn about, so these letters are rearranged
round means surrounding, so the reworked letters enclose the other

explanation.surface: Pining for the reed beds scattered round an island.
explanation.definitionFit: To desire something and to long for it both mean to want it strongly.

clue.text: Inner part of shoe man is seen flourishing round Spain

indicators.note: flourishing means waved about, so these letters are rearranged
round means surrounding, so the reworked letters enclose the other

explanation.surface: A man shows off his Spanish footwear.
explanation.walkthrough: E is Spain's vehicle registration code.
explanation.definitionFit: An inseam is a seam on the inside, as of a shoe upper, so it is an inner part of the shoe.

clue.text: An eighth day, or half a seventh, counting up

indicators.note: only half of the word is kept, its second half dropped
in a down entry, counting up means reading from the bottom, so backwards

blocks.note: the seventh day of the week

explanation.surface: Seems a puzzle in counting days of the week.
explanation.walkthrough: Utas is the octave of a church festival, the eighth day after it counting the feast itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Utas is an old term for the octave of a feast, the eighth day after the festival or the week following it.

clue.text: Outer district of Hungary, part of exurban Attala

indicators.note: part of says the letters are found within the following words

explanation.surface: A suburban fringe region of Hungary named after a place called Attala.
explanation.walkthrough: The Banat was a frontier province of old Hungary.
explanation.definitionFit: The Banat is a historical frontier region once in the Kingdom of Hungary, governed by a ban.

clue.text: Characters heading for the eastern Himalayan range may identify me

definitions.text: Characters heading for the eastern Himalayan range may identify me

indicators.note: characters at the head of each word are their first letters

explanation.surface: A riddle in which a mountain animal asks to be identified by its home range.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the animal, which lives in the eastern Himalayas.
explanation.definitionFit: The tehr, or tahr, is a wild goat native to the Himalayan mountains, so the range identifies it.

clue.text: If old-fashioned schedule about over, here's a rhetorical device

indicators.note: about means around, so one word surrounds the next

blocks.note: an is an archaic word for if

explanation.surface: Seems to talk about an outdated timetable being redone.
explanation.walkthrough: An over is a set of six deliveries in cricket, and 'an' for 'if' survives in Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: Antimetabole is the rhetorical figure that repeats words in reverse order, as in 'eat to live, not live to eat'.

clue.text: Old German cavalry man devoured parrot!

blocks.note: a reiter was a German mounted soldier

explanation.surface: A horseman ate a parrot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parrot' looks like a bird the soldier ate; it is a verb, to repeat.
explanation.definitionFit: To parrot is to repeat words mechanically, and to reiterate is to say again, so the verbs match.

clue.text: Dance turns containing bit of crudity – ugh!

indicators.note: turning round means the dance is read backwards
a bit of the word here is its first letter
containing means holding something inside

blocks.note: a hey is a country dance

explanation.surface: A dance turns a little vulgar, prompting disgust.
explanation.definitionFit: Yech is an interjection of disgust, an informal variant of the same exclamation of revulsion.

clue.text: Cavalry commander left in wild raids Arabia

indicators.note: wild means unruly, so the letters are thrown into a new order
in places the single letter inside the reworked letters

explanation.surface: A cavalry officer left on reckless raids in Arabia.
explanation.walkthrough: A risaldar commanded a troop of Indian cavalry.
explanation.definitionFit: A risaldar was the commander of a troop of cavalry in the British Indian Army, a native officer rank.
